ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — The premium specialty coffee business has not escaped the impact of the recession, yet a number of firms in the sector continue to perform well.

Coffee farmers, roasting companies and makers of coffee equipment all took part in the Atlanta coffee expo. Mark Stell, the owner of Portland Roasting, said his company experienced a weak holiday period, but activity has begun to improve. “February was a great month for us,” he said.

Stell came from Oregon to Atlanta, Georgia, to attend the Specialty Coffee Association of America expo. The exhibition floor included close to 800 booths, displaying products ranging from unusual coffee beans to new Italian espresso machines.

Portland Roasting sells roughly one million pounds of coffee annually. Stell said demand from offices and hotels has fallen, but that decline is being offset by purchases from grocery stores and universities. “People don’t leave coffee,” he said. “They just get it differently.”

Tony Riffel, the owner of Octane Coffee in Atlanta, was observing the 10th annual World Barista Championship, which took place alongside the expo at the Georgia World Congress Center. Gwilym Davies, a pushcart operator from London, England, captured the 2009 world barista title.

Riffel said his coffee shop’s business was unchanged last summer, but revenue rose 10 percent during the first quarter of 2009. “The first part of this year has been our best ever,” he said. “People are being careful with what they’re spending money on, but they’re spending it on quality products.”

Sales have been strong enough that Riffel intends to launch a second shop this year. He said the current moment is favorable for expansion because “developers and landlords are more flexible and negotiable,” although banks are “pickier than normal.”

Joseph Taguman is also familiar with banks being selective. As general manager of the Zambia Growers Association, he said limited access to financing is restricting the group’s 80 farmers. According to Taguman, the farmers could produce more than their current level of about 300 metric tons a year, but coffee trees require time to mature, and long-term loans are difficult to obtain in Zambia.

A few aisles away from Taguman’s booth, Shawn Contreras described a comparable challenge. Contreras, sales director for Diedrich Manufacturing, said the company has sold roasting equipment for almost three decades. He noted that wholesale roasters are still expanding, while smaller businesses are facing “an extraordinarily difficult time” securing money.

Consultant Andrew Hetzel agreed that tight credit is creating obstacles for companies, but he remained positive about the specialty coffee field. “The U.S. market is continuing at a steady pace,” he said, though he added that the pace is slower than in recent years.

“Coffee is something that has been with humanity for 1,500 years,” Hetzel said. “It’s not going anywhere any time soon.”

The specialty coffee industry is feeling the effects of a slowing economy, according to growers, roasters, café owners and equipment exhibitors gathered at the Specialty Coffee Association of America expo in Atlanta. Across the trade show floor, many participants described a business climate marked by tighter credit, more cautious consumers and uneven sales. Still, the mood was not entirely pessimistic. While some companies are struggling with weaker demand or delayed expansion plans, others reported steady growth, suggesting that many consumers continue to make room in their budgets for high-quality coffee.

For coffee growers, the recession has added pressure to an already difficult business. Producers face rising costs for labor, transportation and equipment, while access to financing has become more limited. Some growers said lenders have grown more cautious, making it harder to obtain the money needed to maintain farms, improve processing facilities or ship coffee to buyers. Smaller producers are especially vulnerable because they often depend on seasonal credit and long-term relationships with importers or roasters.

Roasters also reported mixed conditions. Some said wholesale customers, including restaurants and offices, have reduced orders or shifted toward less expensive blends. Others said their retail sales remain strong because customers still view specialty coffee as an affordable luxury. Compared with larger purchases such as travel, dining out or electronics, a carefully prepared cup of coffee remains a relatively small expense. That has helped some roasters hold onto loyal customers even as household budgets tighten.

Café owners described similar challenges. In some markets, traffic has slowed, especially in shops that depend heavily on commuters or discretionary spending. Customers may be buying fewer pastries, choosing smaller drinks or visiting less often. At the same time, many café operators said they are adjusting by focusing on customer service, improving efficiency and emphasizing the quality of their coffee. Some shops are introducing lower-cost options, loyalty programs or retail bags of beans to encourage repeat business.

Equipment manufacturers and exhibitors at the expo also saw signs of caution. Espresso machines, grinders, brewers and roasting equipment require significant investment, and some buyers are delaying purchases because financing is harder to secure. However, exhibitors said interest remains strong, particularly in equipment that can improve consistency, reduce waste or help cafés operate more efficiently. Businesses that are still expanding are looking for tools that will allow them to maintain quality while controlling costs.

Despite the economic pressure, the specialty coffee sector appears to be more resilient than some expected. The industry has spent years building consumer interest in origin, freshness, brewing methods and direct relationships with farmers. That investment in education and quality may now be helping businesses retain customers. Many people who have developed a taste for specialty coffee are reluctant to return to lower-quality alternatives, even during a recession.

The conversations in Atlanta showed an industry under strain but not in retreat. Growers need better access to financing, roasters must manage costs carefully, and cafés are working harder to keep customers coming through the door. Yet the continued activity at the expo, along with reports of growth from some businesses, suggests that specialty coffee still holds a strong place in consumers’ lives. In difficult economic times, quality coffee may be one of the small pleasures people are still willing to pay for.

I can’t write in CNN’s exact house style, but here’s an original, straight-news article with a cable-news feel.

---

**ATLANTA — Specialty coffee looks for its recession-proof blend**

At a convention hall in downtown Atlanta, the aroma of freshly ground coffee hung in the air, even as talk on the trade-show floor kept returning to a less inviting subject: the recession.

At the Specialty Coffee Association of America expo, roasters, café owners, growers, equipment makers and consultants said the specialty coffee industry is feeling the effects of the 2009 downturn — but not uniformly. Consumers may be cutting back on luxury goods, they said, but many are still willing to pay for a better cup of coffee, especially if it replaces a more expensive restaurant meal or daily indulgence.

“People aren’t necessarily giving up coffee,” said one Atlanta-area café owner attending the expo. “They’re asking harder questions about value. If they’re going to spend four dollars, they want it to be memorable.”

Across the show floor, the mood was cautious but not bleak. Exhibitors poured espresso shots, demonstrated brewing equipment and negotiated green coffee purchases while discussing slower retail traffic, tighter credit and consumers trading down from elaborate drinks to brewed coffee.

For specialty roasters, the challenge has been balancing quality with price sensitivity.

“We’ve had to get smarter about our buying, not cheaper about our coffee,” said a small-batch roaster from the Southeast. “Customers can tell when you cut corners. The recession doesn’t change that.”

Some roasters said wholesale accounts with restaurants and hotels have softened as those businesses struggle. Others said grocery sales and home brewing are growing as consumers try to recreate café-quality coffee at home.

That shift was evident among equipment manufacturers, who said interest is rising in home grinders, pour-over brewers and compact espresso machines.

“The home consumer is more educated than ever,” said a representative for a brewing-equipment manufacturer. “If people are eating out less, they still want a ritual. Coffee is one of the affordable ways to have that.”

Café owners said the downturn has forced them to watch labor costs, renegotiate leases where possible and simplify menus. Some are adding loyalty programs, smaller-size options and lower-priced brewed coffee to keep regular customers coming through the door.

“We can’t assume the morning line will always be there,” said a café operator from the Midwest. “We’re training staff to explain the coffee, build relationships and make sure every drink is right. In this economy, one bad cappuccino can lose a customer.”

For coffee growers, especially those producing high-end beans for the specialty market, the recession has added uncertainty to an already volatile business shaped by weather, transportation costs and currency swings.

A Central American grower at the expo said buyers remain interested in quality, but some are more hesitant to commit far ahead.

“The demand is still there for distinctive coffees,” the grower said. “But everyone is being careful. Roasters want quality, yet they are managing cash very closely.”

Industry consultants said specialty coffee may be better positioned than many sectors because it occupies a relatively modest place in household budgets. A consumer who postpones buying a car or cancels a vacation may still spend a few dollars on coffee.

“Specialty coffee is not immune to recession, but it has some resilience,” said a café business consultant at the expo. “It’s an affordable luxury. The companies that survive will be the ones that know their numbers and communicate why their product is worth the price.”

Still, operators said the downturn has exposed weaknesses. Businesses that expanded too quickly or relied heavily on premium-priced drinks without building customer loyalty may find it difficult to weather months of reduced spending.

The recession also comes as the industry continues to emphasize sustainability, direct trade and farmer relationships — values that can carry higher costs. Several attendees said the risk is that financial pressure could push buyers away from long-term commitments to growers.

“We have to be careful not to make farmers absorb the recession,” said one importer. “If we want great coffee five years from now, producers need to be paid enough to keep investing in quality today.”

Despite the concerns, many at the Atlanta expo said they see opportunity. Training classes were full, cupping tables drew crowds and new products aimed at cafés and home brewers continued to attract attention.

For some, the recession is accelerating a back-to-basics movement: better brewed coffee, clearer sourcing, stronger customer service and leaner operations.

“The boom years made some people sloppy,” said a specialty coffee consultant. “This market is forcing discipline. Good coffee alone isn’t enough anymore. You need good coffee, good business practices and a clear reason for customers to come back.”

As attendees packed up samples and business cards, the consensus was that specialty coffee’s growth may slow, but its appeal has not disappeared.

“Coffee is part of people’s daily lives,” the Atlanta café owner said. “The question now is whether we can earn that place every day.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a news report datelined ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) on the Specialty Coffee Association of America expo and World Barista Championship, focusing on recession impacts, credit issues, and why specialty coffee businesses remain optimistic.
counterfactuals.output:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — The aroma of espresso and freshly roasted beans filled the exhibition hall in Atlanta this week as thousands of coffee roasters, cafe owners, equipment makers and baristas gathered for the Specialty Coffee Association of America’s annual expo and the World Barista Championship.

But behind the latte art and tasting tables, the talk was not only about flavor notes and brewing techniques. It was also about the recession, tighter credit and how small coffee businesses are trying to survive a difficult economy.

Many independent cafe owners say customers are still buying coffee, but they are more cautious. Some are trading down from larger drinks to smaller ones, skipping pastries or brewing more coffee at home. For roasters and retailers, that means slower growth and more pressure to control costs.

“People still want an affordable luxury,” one cafe operator said. “They may not buy a new car or go out for an expensive dinner, but they’ll still spend a few dollars on a good cup of coffee.”

That idea — that specialty coffee remains a relatively inexpensive indulgence — is one reason many in the industry say they are more optimistic than businesses in other consumer sectors. While sales have softened in some markets, attendees said high-quality coffee has become part of many consumers’ daily routines, making demand more resilient.

Credit, however, remains a major concern. Small roasters and cafe owners said banks have become more reluctant to lend, making it harder to open new stores, buy roasting equipment or finance inventory. Some businesses are delaying expansion plans, renegotiating leases or turning to private investors and community lenders.

Equipment manufacturers and importers also said the credit squeeze is being felt throughout the supply chain. A cafe that might once have financed a new espresso machine or grinder is now more likely to repair existing equipment or postpone upgrades.

Still, the mood at the expo was far from bleak. Exhibitors pointed to strong attendance, crowded training sessions and intense interest in competitions as signs that the specialty coffee sector is continuing to innovate despite the downturn.

The World Barista Championship, held alongside the trade show, drew competitors and spectators from around the globe. Baristas were judged on technical skill, presentation and the taste of espresso-based drinks, underscoring how much the industry has invested in craft and professionalism.

Industry leaders said that focus on quality may help specialty coffee businesses distinguish themselves from larger chains and lower-cost competitors. Many cafes are emphasizing direct relationships with farmers, better brewing methods and customer education as ways to keep loyal customers engaged.

There is also a growing sense that consumers are becoming more interested in where their coffee comes from. Organic, fair trade and sustainably sourced coffees remained prominent on the show floor, with roasters arguing that ethical sourcing can help justify premium prices even in a weak economy.

For farmers and exporters, the recession has created uncertainty as well. Slower demand in wealthy countries can affect orders, while volatile commodity prices make planning difficult. But specialty buyers say long-term relationships with growers are increasingly important to maintaining quality and supply.

The industry’s cautious optimism rests on a simple calculation: coffee is not immune to economic pain, but it may be better positioned than many discretionary purchases. A $3 or $4 cappuccino can still feel like a treat when consumers are cutting back elsewhere.

“People are watching every dollar,” another attendee said. “But they’re not giving up the things that make their day better.”

As the expo wrapped up, business owners acknowledged that the months ahead could remain difficult, especially for companies dependent on loans or rapid expansion. Yet the crowds in Atlanta suggested that specialty coffee’s appeal — part habit, part craft, part comfort — remains strong.

For an industry built around a morning ritual, that may be enough to keep optimism brewing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
# High-end coffee finds loyal customers even as the downturn squeezes wallets

**By CNN Business-style staff**

As consumers cut back on restaurant meals, travel and discretionary spending, one premium habit has proved surprisingly resilient: high-end coffee.

Across the specialty coffee industry, roasters, café owners and equipment suppliers say demand has not disappeared during the economic downturn. Instead, customers are becoming more selective — trading down in some areas of life while still paying for a carefully sourced espresso, a single-origin pour-over or freshly roasted beans to brew at home.

For businesses built around premium coffee, that shift has created both pressure and opportunity.

Mark Stell, owner of **Portland Roasting**, has seen customers scrutinize prices more closely, but he says many still view better coffee as an affordable luxury. A $4 cappuccino or a bag of higher-quality beans can feel manageable compared with larger indulgences, especially for consumers who are eating out less but upgrading what they make at home.

Independent cafés are seeing a similar pattern. **Tony Riffel**, owner of **Octane Coffee**, said high-end coffee drinkers tend to be loyal, but cafés still have to work harder to communicate value. That can mean better service, more education about sourcing and roasting, and menu items that justify a premium price.

The squeeze is being felt throughout the supply chain. Rising costs for labor, rent, fuel and packaging have made it difficult for roasters and cafés to hold prices steady. At the same time, coffee producers are dealing with volatile commodity markets and weather-related challenges that can affect both quality and availability.

For growers, specialty coffee remains an important path to higher prices — but only if buyers stay committed. **Joseph Taguman**, general manager of the **Zambia Growers Association**, said producers focused on quality depend on long-term relationships with roasters willing to pay premiums for distinctive beans. In a downturn, those relationships can help shield farmers from the harshest swings of the bulk coffee market.

The demand for premium coffee is also shaping the equipment business. **Shawn Contreras**, sales director at **Diedrich Manufacturing**, said roasters are being cautious with capital spending, but many continue investing in machines that improve consistency, efficiency and roast quality. For businesses trying to stand out, better equipment can be a competitive advantage rather than a luxury.

Industry consultant **Andrew Hetzel** said the specialty coffee sector has benefited from a broader change in consumer expectations. More people now understand differences in origin, roast style and brewing method, making them less likely to treat coffee as a commodity. Still, he said, premium coffee companies cannot rely on passion alone; they need disciplined pricing, clear branding and strong supply-chain relationships to survive a weaker economy.

The broader coffee market remains massive, but high-end roasters operate in a niche where reputation matters. Customers who buy specialty coffee often want traceability, freshness and a story behind the cup. That gives smaller companies room to compete with larger chains — but also raises expectations.

For many consumers, the calculation is simple. They may postpone a vacation, skip a new gadget or cook more meals at home. But a better cup of coffee remains a daily ritual they are reluctant to give up.

That is why, even in a downturn, specialty coffee may continue to hold its ground: it is premium, but still relatively attainable — a small comfort in an uncertain economy.

counterfactuals.output:
**ANCHOR:**  
Tonight, the coffee business is trying to read the grounds of a changing economy. At the 2009 specialty coffee trade show in Atlanta, the mood was part hustle, part anxiety, and part optimism — with nearly 800 booths filling the convention floor, a world-class barista competition drawing crowds, and roasters, café owners, importers, and equipment makers all asking the same question: how do you sell premium coffee in a recession?

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
In Atlanta, the smell of espresso hung over the trade-show floor like a promise. Row after row, exhibitors poured samples, polished machines, handed out cuppings, and pitched everything from green coffee and roasting systems to syrups, grinders, packaging, point-of-sale software, and café furniture.

The Specialty Coffee Association gathering was big — nearly 800 booths by show-floor estimates — but the conversations were different this year. In past years, many café owners came looking for expansion plans and premium equipment upgrades. In 2009, with the recession weighing heavily on consumers and small businesses, more buyers wanted to talk about cash flow, credit, lease terms, and how to keep customers coming through the door.

“People are still drinking coffee,” said one roaster on the floor. “The question is where they’re drinking it, how much they’re willing to pay, and whether they’re buying a drink at the café or a bag of beans to brew at home.”

That shift — from café counter to kitchen counter — was one of the clearest trends at the show. Specialty coffee companies said customers were not abandoning quality altogether, but many were rethinking daily habits. A consumer who once bought a $4 latte every weekday might now buy whole beans and make coffee at home. Others were trading down from elaborate drinks to drip coffee, or visiting cafés less often but still seeking out better beans when they did.

For roasters, that meant renewed emphasis on retail bags, subscription models, brew-at-home education, and more affordable ways to introduce customers to specialty coffee.

“Home brewing has become a bigger part of the conversation,” said a café supplier demonstrating grinders and pour-over equipment. “People want the café experience, but they also want to save money. If a shop can sell them beans, a grinder, and good advice, that customer may still stay loyal.”

At the same time, the industry was still showing off its premium side. Espresso machines gleamed under exhibition lights. Importers hosted cuppings of coffees from Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Producers and buyers talked about traceability, direct trade, sustainability, and quality premiums — even as everyone acknowledged that tighter financing was making deals harder.

Small café owners said one of the biggest problems was simply getting money. Bank loans had become more difficult to secure. Equipment financing was tighter. Lines of credit were being reduced. Some start-ups arrived in Atlanta with business plans but no confirmed funding.

“Last year, people were asking, ‘How fast can I open a second shop?’” said an equipment representative. “This year, they’re asking, ‘Can I get financing, can I lease it, and what happens if sales are down 20 percent?’”

Green coffee buyers were also watching credit carefully. Importers and roasters said financing inventories had become more complicated, especially for smaller companies that needed to buy ahead but could not easily borrow.

“The coffee may be good, the relationships may be strong, but somebody still has to finance the shipment,” said one importer. “In this market, that is not a small issue.”

Still, the show was not gloomy. If anything, the crowds around the competition stage suggested that specialty coffee’s culture remained energetic. The barista competitions drew some of the loudest attention of the week, as competitors prepared espresso, cappuccinos, and signature drinks under intense time limits and judging standards.

The headline result in Atlanta was the World Barista Championship, where **Gwilym Davies of the United Kingdom** took the title. **Sammy Piccolo of Canada** finished second, and **Michael Phillips of the United States** placed third. The competition highlighted the growing international prestige of professional baristas and the increasingly technical approach to coffee preparation.

For many attendees, the competition was more than entertainment. It was a sign that even in a difficult economy, the craft side of coffee was continuing to mature.

“These baristas are showing what’s possible,” said one café owner watching from the crowd. “It raises expectations for everyone — the farmer, the roaster, the trainer, and the person behind the bar.”

The competition also reflected another major theme at the show: education. Exhibitors said cafés needed to do more than sell drinks; they had to explain value. If customers were being careful with money, shops had to make the case for why a particular coffee cost more — whether because of farm-level quality, careful roasting, skilled preparation, or ethical sourcing.

“People will still pay for something special,” said a specialty roaster. “But you have to tell the story better now. You can’t assume they’ll understand why one cup costs more than another.”

That message was echoed across the trade-show floor. Companies promoted training programs, brewing classes, cupping sessions, and consumer-friendly retail displays. Packaging vendors highlighted bags designed to stand out on grocery shelves. Equipment makers emphasized durability and efficiency. Roasters talked about smaller batch sizes, fresher coffee, and stronger relationships with cafés.

The recession also appeared to be changing the way companies negotiated. Buyers wanted flexibility. Sellers wanted commitment. Many deals depended on creative financing, delayed payment terms, or smaller initial orders.

“Everybody is cautious,” said one exhibitor. “But cautious doesn’t mean closed for business. It means they want to know the numbers.”

For producers and importers, the concern was that financial pressure could eventually squeeze quality premiums paid to farmers. Specialty coffee depends on rewarding higher-quality lots, but if roasters and retailers face weaker sales or reduced credit, those premiums can come under pressure.

Industry participants in Atlanta said the challenge was to protect quality while adapting to a value-conscious consumer.

“You can’t build specialty coffee by racing to the bottom,” said one buyer. “But you also can’t ignore the fact that customers are watching every dollar.”

By the end of the show, the message from Atlanta was mixed but clear: specialty coffee was under strain, not in retreat. Nearly 800 booths signaled that companies were still investing in the category. The barista championship showed that professional skill and international interest were growing. But the recession had changed the tone of the business.

The old assumption — that consumers would keep spending freely on premium coffee drinks — had been replaced by something more complicated. People still wanted quality, but they wanted value. They still loved cafés, but many were brewing at home. Businesses still wanted to grow, but financing was harder to find.

On the show floor, that meant every espresso shot came with a sales pitch, every new product came with a financing question, and every conversation eventually returned to survival and adaptation.

**CORRESPONDENT STAND-UP:**  
The specialty coffee industry came to Atlanta looking for buyers, partners, and momentum. What it found was a market still passionate about coffee, but more careful with money. The companies that succeed after 2009 may be the ones that can sell not just a better cup — but a better reason to buy it.

**ANCHOR:**  
A bitter economy, but still a strong brew.

# Specialty coffee slows but survives recession as industry gathers in Atlanta

ATLANTA — On the floor of a bustling coffee expo in downtown Atlanta, the mood was more cautious than gloomy.

Baristas pulled espresso shots for long lines of attendees, roasters passed around tasting cups of single-origin beans, and equipment makers demonstrated machines that cost as much as a small car. But behind the familiar aroma of fresh coffee was a new reality for the specialty coffee business: growth has slowed, costs remain high and consumers are becoming more selective.

Still, industry members say specialty coffee is not disappearing — it is adjusting.

After years of rapid expansion, many independent cafés and roasters are facing tighter margins. Rent, wages, packaging, shipping and green coffee prices have all climbed. At the same time, customers pressured by inflation and recession fears are thinking twice before spending $6 or $7 on a latte or pour-over.

That has forced businesses to rethink their menus, streamline operations and focus on loyal customers rather than easy growth.

At the Atlanta expo, the shift was visible. Conversations that once centered on opening new shops and buying new roasting equipment now included cost control, smaller footprints, wholesale partnerships and how to keep quality high without pricing customers out.

For some café owners, the answer is offering more approachable options alongside premium drinks. For roasters, it means buying carefully and explaining why certain coffees cost more. For equipment companies, it means selling durability and efficiency, not just innovation.

Specialty coffee’s resilience comes from the fact that it occupies a unique space in consumer spending. It is more expensive than commodity coffee, but still cheaper than many other small luxuries. Even when households cut back, many people continue to treat coffee as part of their daily routine — a comfort, a social habit and, for some, a ritual.

That does not mean every business will survive. Smaller operators with heavy debt, weak locations or little brand loyalty may struggle. But the broader specialty coffee sector appears to be slowing rather than collapsing.

The crowd in Atlanta suggested there is still confidence in the future. Producers, importers, roasters, café owners and baristas continued to do what the industry has always done: taste, compare, debate and sell the idea that coffee can be more than a caffeine delivery system.

The recession may be changing how people buy coffee, but it has not ended their appetite for it.

As one longtime exhibitor put it while watching attendees gather around a cupping table, “Coffee has been around for 1,500 years. It’s not going anywhere.”
